about: Corrections to the research facts, applied by tools/compile_facts.py. Each names the fact key, what changes and why; text replacements are asserted against the current notes, so none fails silently. Sources: the verifier checks in research/round1/verify_<topic>.json and this session's own reading.

corrections.why: The fact is an assumption with no source (its own source title says so), but the researcher attached an unrelated Europe PMC search URL to it. Removed the URL so the page does not show a link as if it were a source.

corrections.append_notes: Change to: 'Burton 2018 (Children) is peer-reviewed. Burton 2010 is a Medical Hypotheses paper published before that journal adopted peer review in 2010 (editor-selected): argument plus modelling.' corrections.append_notes: Replace 'none found' with: 'No published FFM/H^3 muscularity index for adults was found, but Forbes's model FFM = 10.3 x H^3 (reported by Wang et al. 2012) and Wang's fit FFM = 10.8 x H^2.95 (males aged 5-59, CI 2.83-3.07) are published precedent for FFM proportional to H^3 across growth. corrections.why:
Verifier (index): Wells & Cole 2002 (FFM/HT^2 optimal, FM/HT^6, n = 69, deuterium) and Ramirez-Velez 2018 (n = 4673, fat mass/height^3) check out. The researcher's ABSTRACT-field phrase searches do return 0, as stated.

corrections.append_notes: Use the label 'On average, taller adults have lower girth-to-height ratios (regression powers below 1)'. Status: measured for the regression numbers, but put the structural reading under the disputed key height_exponent_regression_vs_isometry, citing Burton 2010's counter-claim on girths. Note that waist and hip mostly reflect fat.
corrections.why:
Verifier (index): The numbers check out:
- Burton 2012 abstract: 155 men, 162 women, P = 0.00006-0.027.

(a) These are regression powers. Burton 2010, which the researcher cites, argues that regression underestimates structural exponents. It says girth data 'are

set.label: On average, taller adults have lower girth-to-height ratios (regression powers below 1); whether that is structural is disputed

corrections.append_notes: Label: 'Sport science normalises performance for body size allometrically. Exponents come either from geometric similarity (Jaric's proposal: 0.67 for force) or from fitting to data (Nevill 1992: about 2/3 for VO2max and power).' Add: 'Applied to FFM against adult height, the empirical approach gives about 2 (FFMI); geometric similarity gives 3. These papers cover performance, not body composition.'
